questions.title: Is QLoRA actually performing 4-bit matrix multiplication?
questions.question_body: I am confused about the distinction between 'storage data type' and 'computation data type' mentioned in the paper. The authors state that the model is quantized to 4-bit, but then they say that whenever a weight tensor is used, it is dequantized to BFloat16 to perform the matrix multiplication. If the actual math is happening in 16-bit, does this mean there is no computational speedup from the 4-bit quantization, and the benefit is strictly related to GPU memory capacity?

questions.title: What makes NormalFloat (NF4) 'information theoretically optimal'?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) and claims it is information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights. I understand that it uses quantiles of a $N(0, 1)$ distribution to define the bins, but I don't understand why this is superior to standard 4-bit integers (Int4) or floats (FP4). Specifically, how does ensuring each bin has an equal number of values assigned from the input tensor reduce quantization error in practice?

questions.title: How does the memory saving calculation for Double Quantization work?
questions.question_body: In the Double Quantization section, the authors mention that for a blocksize of 64, the memory footprint of quantization constants is reduced from $32/64 = 0.5$ bits per parameter to $8/64 + 32/(64 \cdot 256) = 0.127$ bits. I'm struggling to follow this math. Why is the second term divided by $64 \cdot 256$, and what exactly does the $8/64$ represent in the context of the second quantization step?

questions.title: How does backpropagation work through frozen 4-bit weights?
questions.question_body: The paper states that QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained model into the LoRA adapters. Since the weights $\mathbf{W}^{NF4}$ are frozen and quantized (which is a non-differentiable operation), I'm confused about how the gradient $\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{L}_i}$ is calculated. Does the gradient simply flow through the dequantized $\mathbf{W}^{BF16}$ as if it were a standard constant weight, or is there something special about the backward pass in the CUDA kernels?

questions.title: Why is the number of adapter layers more critical than the rank $r$?
questions.question_body: In Section 4, the authors find that the most critical LoRA hyperparameter for matching 16-bit performance is the number of adapters used (applying them to all linear layers), while the projection dimension $r$ has little effect. This is surprising to me because the rank $r$ usually determines the capacity of the adapter. Why would adding adapters to more layers be more effective for recovering quantization loss than increasing the rank of a few adapters?
